title: EU methane regulation risks worsening the energy crisis | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie argues EU Methane Regulation Article 28, applying from 1 January 2027, could leave only 57% of gas/LNG and about 13% of crude imports compliant, worsening Europe's winter energy crisis; a one-year delay is expected but may not suffice.

insights.claim: Article 28 of the EU Methane Emissions Regulation, scheduled to apply from 1 January, requires non-EU oil and gas importers to meet methane measurement, reporting and verification equivalence with EU producers, and threatens to cut oil and gas imports into Europe while supply is already constrained by the Iran and Russia/Ukraine wars.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Policy-driven import shortfall stacks on top of geopolitical supply shocks; watch EU gas and diesel pricing into winter.
insights.quote: Well-intentioned regulation agreed over two years ago now looks ill-timed and, increasingly, a self-inflicted wound

insights.claim: Penalties for non-compliance with the EU methane import rules are severe, at up to 20% of an importer's global annual revenues, so importers are unwilling to accept non-compliance risk.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Penalty size makes importers likely to avoid unverified cargoes rather than gamble, tightening supply.

insights.claim: Most oil and gas exporting countries outside Europe are not ready to meet EU methane MRV equivalence within the timeframe, and no agency is yet accredited to verify methane measurement and reporting of production outside the EU.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The missing verification infrastructure is the binding constraint, so compliant supply can't scale quickly.
insights.locator: But the regulations are not workable at present

insights.claim: Traded LNG and oil cargoes already at sea pose a particular compliance challenge, raising the risk that LNG tankers could be unable to land unverified cargoes in mid-winter.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A cargo-rejection scenario would be a sharp upside risk for European gas prices.
insights.quote: Could LNG tankers be left out at sea in mid-winter, unable to land their unverified cargoes?
insights.locator: But the regulations are not workable at present

insights.claim: In Wood Mackenzie's Default scenario, with the regulation enforced as written, only 57% of 2024 EU gas and LNG import volumes would be compliant on 1 January 2027.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Over 40% of 2024-level gas import volumes at risk of exclusion implies major price and security-of-supply stress.
insights.locator: Analysing the impact of compliance on imports

insights.claim: An Adaptive scenario that prioritises security of supply and gives flexibility to 10 key exporting countries lifts gas and LNG compliance to 80%, which is better but still far from averting a crisis.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Even a softened implementation leaves a 20% compliance gap.
insights.locator: Analysing the impact of compliance on imports

insights.claim: In the Default scenario, compliant crude supply could fall to around 13% of the EU's total 2024 crude imports, threatening the foundations of European refining.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Severe crude sourcing constraints are bearish for EU refiners and bullish for refined-product tightness.
insights.quote: putting the very foundations of European refining under threat
insights.locator: Analysing the impact of compliance on imports

insights.claim: Industry players and 17 EU member states have asked for a three-year postponement of the most substantive Article 28 requirements.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Broad political pressure raises odds of a delay.

insights.claim: The Commission has so far suggested member states waive financial penalties through end-2029, but this does not waive the reporting obligation, so importers still face legal liability under the primary legislation.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The penalty holiday gives incomplete relief, so importer behaviour may stay cautious.

insights.claim: French President Macron asked Commission President von der Leyen for a one-year delay, pushing Article 28's start to 1 January 2028, framed around Hormuz-driven price pressure and cost-of-living politics; Wood Mackenzie expects the Commission to accede.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A delay is the base case; trade on a delay announcement easing winter risk premia.
insights.quote: We expect the European Commission to accede to the French request.

insights.claim: Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen this week indicated a possible 12-month delay to the regulation's implementation.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Official signalling supports the delay thesis.

themes.theme: European gas and oil market tightness

insights.claim: European gas is already tight: spot prices are at a multi-year high, storage is tracking to just 71% against an 80% end-October target, and little or no new LNG supply comes onstream until the second half of 2027.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Thin buffers mean any compliance-driven supply loss hits prices hard.
insights.locator: Why a one-year delay may not be enough

insights.claim: Adding MER non-compliance risk could push European and Asian traded gas prices this winter close to their peak after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Winter gas price upside tail is material if the rules are not delayed.
insights.locator: Why a one-year delay may not be enough

insights.claim: Constrained supply has already pushed European diesel from around EUR 1.60/L to record levels, and the regulation risks pushing refined product prices higher and accelerating refinery closures, hurting energy security and jobs.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Watch diesel cracks and EU refinery closure announcements.
insights.locator: Why a one-year delay may not be enough

insights.claim: A 12-month delay would still leave MRV compliance a genuine challenge for many importers, but would improve the chances imports keep the EU supplied through overlapping crises.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A one-year delay is a partial fix only; the compliance problem resurfaces in 2028.
insights.quote: Good intentions, badly timed, can still do real damage.
insights.locator: Why a one-year delay may not be enough
